key_idea: Removing one bar multiplies the resulting permutation by a transposition, so the minimum number of removals is w minus the number of cycles of the current permutation; maintain that permutation with a segment tree over heights.
sketch: Lower bound: deleting a bar swaps the two endpoints of the paths that crossed there, changing the cycle count by exactly one, so at least w - cycles removals are needed. Achievable: in any non-trivial cycle some two of its paths must swap relative order, which can only happen at a bar they both use, and deleting that bar splits the cycle. Build a segment tree over the h heights where each leaf holds identity or an adjacent transposition and each node the composition of its children (top first, T[i] = R[L[i]]). Each toggle recomputes log h nodes at O(w) each, then count cycles of the root in O(w): O(q w log h) total, about 7e7 basic operations. Verified against an exponential subset brute force on 300 random small cases. Pitfalls: composition order is not commutative, store permutations as bytes (2^19 nodes * 20 bytes) to keep memory small.
